7.17.m: The god stretched out his hands, having rested his knees and his water-pot; / with extended rays he became like the sun shining in the sky. (28) / Having recited the supreme prayer born of the essence of the three Vedas, / Bhava, skillful [and] with his four faces, began to dance dexterously. (29) / Seeing her husband dancing with tender sprout-like hands swaying, / the goddess, his companion in sacred duty, danced along with her husband. (30) / Seeing the couple dancing with loud bursts of laughter, the leader of the gaṇas, / Nandī, then danced, bringing delight to both deities. (31) / Seeing the god and the Mother dancing, and Nandī as well, / the pramathas, resembling dark blue clouds, danced to the sounds of musical instruments. (32) / Then kettledrums and jharjharas, kikhiras, ānakas, and maṇḍukas, / āḍambaras, small drums, and conchs sounded forth. (33) / Again and again Ambikā accomplished a skillful dance; / Nandī gave vent to laughter, and the fierce pramathas roared aloud. (34) / Filled with the sounds of those excellent musical instruments, tumultuous with the noise of Śiva's thunderbolt, / the onset of twilight blazed terribly like the mouth of the submarine fire. (35) / Some danced, others laughed, and others muttered prayers; / yet others among the attendants sang very sweetly, like gandharvas. (36) / Then, as the moon, the crest of the vault of the sky, with full disk and exceedingly clear, / the deer-marked one, had risen, [he who is] adorned with the crescent moon (37)

concluded his observance, accompanied by Ambā, Nandīśa, and his attendants. / The god ceased from that festivity and addressed Pārvatī thus: (38)
"Having spent this night, O night of immeasurable prowess, / tomorrow you shall then receive that son, the little Aśoka tree." (39) / Holding to the earth covered with darbha grass, that supporter of the earth, / following the god's command, slept for one night, keeping her vow. (40) / Then, when the hundred-thousand-rayed sun arose, [Śiva,] creator of the sun, / said to Umā: "Let us go to where that Aśoka, your son, is." (41)
Then the blessed one, fortunate, bestower of wealth, worshipped by the lord of wealth, / whose ornaments tinkled, said to Bhava: "Let us go." (42) / On foot, the blessed Hara, whose abode is at the foot of trees, / accompanied by Nandī and Ambikā, approached that Aśoka tree. (43) / There he saw the tawny yakṣa, who was like a reddish-yellow fire, / preparing food along with the pramathas, the provider of food. (44)

Sanatkumāra said:
Then the lord of the mountain, the remover of the distress of those bowed before him, granting desires, / said to the daughter of the king of mountains: "Look upon these mountains of food!" (52) / Seeing those mountain-like elevations of food to be chewed and swallowed, / the queen of the gods, the fire-stick that produced Guha, was deeply pleased with Piṅgala. (53) / The daughter of the mountain favored Sumālin, that best of yakṣas, Piṅgala, / by granting a boon; and Maheśvara spoke to her: (54) / "O goddess, all this excellent food to be chewed and swallowed is prepared for you; / do that task which you desire. Why do you sit idle?" (55) / Then she, exceedingly delighted, clothed in celestial garments, / taking leave of Śaṅkara, the lord of the universe, swift as thought, (56) / that night-like goddess who brings grief to the Daityas, / decorated that Aśoka tree with affection, using various kinds of ornaments. (57) / And before it the daughter of the mountain raised a parasol / shining with strings of pearls, along with peacock feathers. (58) / And with fragrant sandalwood of various colors, / the goddess marked its trunk from the very root with an excellent paste. (59)

And with cloths of gold adorned with jewels,
she decorated the beloved aśoka sapling on all sides.
On its branches and twigs Pārvatī
bound strings of pearls; with them it shone like the moon with the constellations.
Then with pairs of white garments the mother of the worlds,
the mother of Guha, longing for a son, clothed that aśoka tree.
Then the granter of boons to the gods offered blended incense:
turpentine resin, nameru, bdellium, and clarified butter.
Then, with the sounding of conches and the fanfare of divine musical instruments,
the wife of the mighty one, performing her austerity, offered an oblation.

7.17.m:
As she thus worshiped that tree, which had the luster of nectar and a necklace of moons,
milk flowed from both her breasts because of her maternal affection.
Worshiped by Umā, that aśoka tree illuminating the forest
shone exceedingly there, like Spring personified.
Then, having given what they desired to the brahmins brought by Nandin,
who were equal to Brahmā, she had them pronounce the blessing of an auspicious day.
Then, at the conclusion of the proclamation of the auspicious day and of the benediction of both,
having obtained her husband's consent, the goddess said to those seers:
“Venerable ones, I who am childless will adopt this aśoka sapling
as a son today; you ought to grant your permission.”
To the goddess Pārvatī who was speaking thus, yearning for a son,
all the twice-born said with one voice: “Let him be taken as you desire!”
Then a celestial sounding of conches, accompanied by the blare of all musical instruments,
rang out, filling all three steps of Nārāyaṇa.

7.17.m:
The overjoyed gods watched that festival of the aśoka sapling,
where the music of the gandharvas sounded and troops of apsarases danced vigorously.
Playing the Kacchapī lute, the foremost of lute-players,
Nārada danced out of joy, like a fire driven by the wind.
Worshiped there by the rich in austerity, by the gods, and by Kubera,
[the goddess] shone like the radiance of the sun.
Then, having completed her vow and taken the aśoka sapling as a son,
the daughter of the lord of mountains shone like the earth sprinkled with water.
Then, instructed by Nandīśvara, those pramathas by the thousands,
affectionate toward brahmins, quickly brought their seats for the brahmins.
As the seats made of gold, silver, and radiant crystal
were spread out by the pramathas, a great noise arose,

A continuous row of seats was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
on the auspicious ridge of Mount Mandara, rows of brahmins extended forth.
[…] all risen like suns […].
Those adornments of seats shone like […] when bathed;
those thousands of rows [spread] on the vast Mount Mandara.
Having summoned the twice-born who were anointed with a mixture of yakṣa-paste,
adorned with crest-jewels and wearing garlands of flowers, and eager […],
with mandāra, saṃtāna, and pāribhadra blossoms,
and [cooled] by breezes […], the twice-born shone like gods.
Then, strewn all around by the gods with very smooth, fragrant,
and yellowish scented powders,
marked with paste of celestial sandalwood and sprinkled with celestial powders,

7.17.m:
Having spread divine incense everywhere on my command, / then [water] resembling crystal was gathered like lotus pollen; / in a moment, water for washing the hands was given by Śaṃkara's servants. / Then, with girded loins, like brave elephants with girded girths, / the Pramathas began to serve the foremost of brahmins. / Then the gods, acting humbly, in a moment gave / gold, silver, and crystal vessels to the twice-born.
Drawing and carrying water in vessels […], / they duly offered foods to chew and eat, along with drinks, on all sides. / Rich in substance […] / what was in their eyes, what was in their hearts, what was in their mouths, and what was signaled by their hands—

7.17.m:
Kustumburu, Śāliśiras, Parjanya, Gaṇḍamaṇḍaka, / Citrāṅgada, Citrasena, Citra, and Citraratha— / these celestial gandharvas, who had struck their instruments and were dear to Hara, / sang in divine notes a song awakening love. / Nameru mixed with bdellium, sprinkled with streams of ghee— / that supreme incense was spread there by the doorkeepers,
for whose sake this verse, marked with the three incenses, wanders / in the three steps of Nārāyaṇa, worshipped by the gods along with Indra. / Of bdellium, of nameru, and indeed of ghee-incense, / the gods could not get enough, as from the sight of their beloveds.
The winds did not abandon their movement / amidst the three incenses: / of bdellium, of nameru, and of ghee-incense.
Seeing that festival of the tree, the moon-crested Lord, / who brings joy to Pārvatī, cherished supreme joy again and again.

7.17.m:
[Apparatus readings]
When Paśupati rejoiced, Hara, the lord of vows, again and again, / the three worlds, both moving and unmoving, rejoiced in Paśupati. / Filled with dancing troupes of apsarases, perfumed with divine incense, / strewn with the flowers of the seasons, that assembly resembled the sky. / Then quickly [they served] boiled rice of white grain […]. / With that [food] like ambrosia, all the best of the twice-born, / honoured by the world, were satisfied with food to chew and eat, and with drink.
Then the holy, pleasant-sounding proclamation of "An Auspicious Day!", / which frightens rākṣasas and asuras, was uttered by the brahmins, filling the three worlds.

Then, having greeted with blessings accompanied by flowers and unbroken grains / him, together with Ambā, free from sorrow, with Hara, and with Nandin, / all the great brahmins, pleasant-voiced, wearing the sacred thread and matted locks, / bowed to Virūpākṣa and departed as they had come. / And the gods, honoured by the Trident-holder with gifts and words of welcome, / departed as they had come, surrounding Indra.
The gaṇas, honoured by the guardian of the gaṇas together with the gaṇa leaders, / all went to their respective abodes, shaking their garments in delight: / "Ah, the good fortune of the goddess! Ah, Hara is her beloved! / Ah, we have observed the zeal of the god for the sake of the goddess!
If a woman is not dear to her husband as the daughter of the mountain is to the Lord, / how can she be called fortunate, and why does she even bear womanhood?

the source of speech, said to her husband, the master of the host of beings: // 123

since I have adopted an Aśoka tree as a son. // 124

7.17.m:
The entire three worlds, collectively and individually, O creator of the world,
assembled by your power at the celebration for my tree-son. // 125
Surely it is my good deed, O Lord, my supreme and radiant austerity,
that you, O God, the lord of all beings, have been obtained by me as husband. // 126
And whatever fruit of a wished-for son was previously stolen by the gods,
all of that [loss] has departed from me, having obtained the Aśoka tree as a son. // 127

I whose husband is the lord of vows, a hero, [namely] you, O Maheśvara.” // 128

Having spoken thus with love to Bhava, Bhavānī, wearing a string of pearls,
fell at the Lord’s feet, her eyes filled with tears. // 129
Raising her up and embracing her closely,
placing [...] upon his thighs, the Lord of the Mountain spoke this with affection: // 8.162.130
“O Goddess, faithful, virtuous, and companion in my sacred duties,
pious towards brahmins and offering refuge, you are ever dear to me, O beloved! // 131
Even what should not be done must certainly be done by me for your sake, O Goddess;
how much more that which is combined with glory and endowed with righteousness? // 132
The brahmins have been gratified by you, O Goddess, and so too the gods along with the Gaṇas;
and this little son, the Aśoka tree, has been adopted by you, O beloved. // 133

Come, Goddess, let us go home; your desire is fulfilled.
We shall see that son again, adorned with clusters of flowers.” // 134
Addressed thus by her husband, the virtuous lady, her face and eyes filled with joy,
she of fawn-like eyes spoke these words there to Harita: // 135
“O fawn-eyed one, protect with care this little son standing here,
this good son, O Hari, from elephants, horses, and birds! // 136
And when this little Aśoka son
becomes adorned with clusters of flowers, then you must come see me.” // 137
Having thus instructed Harita, she of startled fawn-like eyes,
casting a sidelong glance, entered her abode
with her husband, as radiance enters the solar disc. // 138
Thus, together with the Lord of Beings, having adopted the sapling Aśoka tree as her son,
the Goddess, standing amid the delighted Gaṇas, then entered her own home with a joyful heart. // 139

This I wish to know through your grace, O great sage. // 3
Thus requested by Vyāsa of unwearied actions,
the best of speakers, the son of the Grandfather, then spoke. // 4
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, even the radiant Fire was not able to hold
that fiery energy of the Three-Eyed Lord, born from the desire for a son. // 5
Though himself of the nature of burning [all] beings, being burned by that fiery energy,
he implored the Gaṅgā to hold that energy. // 6
Implored by that Fire, the goddess who flows through the three worlds,
said in a sweet voice, with apprehension: “So be it.” // 7
Then the splendid carrier of oblations, by his mystic power,
transferred that energy of the God of gods into the Gaṅgā. // 8
Although knowing it was hard to bear, that fair-faced one, the best of rivers,
accepted it, fearing the fault of breaking an applicant's entreaty. // 9
Then, through the power of that fiery energy, she quickly became slow and languid in her gait,
with the nipples of her breasts darkening. // 8.163.10

7.17.m:
Seeing him then, the Kṛttikās, their heavy breasts oozing milk, / came near to him […]. // 17
And the Vedas with the Upavedas and summaries attended upon him, / and all the arts and sciences, Lakṣmī, Medhā, and Sarasvatī, // 18
Loveliness, righteousness, compassion, forbearance, fortitude, patience, valor, / yoga, fiery energy, strength, wisdom, steadfastness, profundity, and good works. // 19
Then, taking up a celestial bow, he of wondrous prowess, / effortlessly fitting an arrow, shot it at the mountain […]. // 20
Sundered suddenly by it, the supreme peak of the mountain fell at once, / its birds terrified, frightened, and flying about in panic. // 21
Seeing that great wonder, both astonishment and fear / arose simultaneously among the creatures dwelling there. // 22
Then, perceiving danger to himself from him, the slayer of Bala / dispatched the mothers for the destruction of the one of boundless splendor. // 23

7.17.m:
Seeing the gods approaching, the greatly splendid one roared aloud, / and rushed at them enraged, like a lion against elephants in rut. // 26
At that roar, the celestials were bewildered again and again; / even on Airāvaṇa’s temples the rutting-juice dried away. // 27
And the son of the three-eyed Lord, destroyer of the gods' pride, / loosed thousands of blazing flames upon those gods. // 28
With their luster struck down by the flames, the faces of the enemies of the asuras / became like lotuses burnt by frost in the lakes. // 29

Then, seizing his flashing thunderbolt, Śatakratu, / the corners of his eyes reddened with wrath, hurled it at the one of fire-like brilliance. // 30
By that blow of the thunderbolt, he then took two forms, / and with both forms he rushed against Purandara. // 31
Then, quickly abandoning his pride, the chastiser of Pāka bowed / to that receptacle of fiery energies, and, completely subdued, spoke thus: // 32
“Accept even this sovereignty, sought after by the high-minded; / you alone are fit for the protection of the worlds, O son of the fire! // 33

[…],” / smiling, the foremost of the mighty replied to the lord of the gods: // 35

Hearing that speech of Skanda whose mind was free from distress, / Śacī's husband again spoke smooth and meaningful words: // 37
[…] // 38
“Show us the manifold, wondrous tasks
joined together, distinct […], / the assumption of the sovereignty of the three worlds, well-ordered and imperishable.” // 39

7.17.m:
The glorious lord of the worlds, the imperishable one, has authority over me,
the incomparable being of immeasurable self whose banner bears the bull, O Purandara.
847
Having worshipped that Lord with devotion, receive his command, O Śatakratu.
Whatever the Lord shall give, that I will undertake.
Understanding his intention, the god of gods whose emblem is the bull
then arrived with his wife, wishing to see his son.
Fire accompanied by Svāhā, Gaṅgā the best of rivers,
and the Kṛttikās, exceedingly delighted, [came to] Śveta, the best of peaks.

7.17.m:
Simultaneously arriving there at that time on the highest peak of Śveta,
they thought: 'Whom indeed will Skanda approach?'
Then, knowing the intention of those wise ones, the best of the intelligent,
Skanda, the lord of yogins, mightily became sixfold.
Skanda approached Mahādeva; Viśākha [went to] the daughter of Himavat;
Naigameṣa went to Gaṅgā; and Śākha of great splendour [went] to Fire.
Overjoyed, Guha, wearing locks of hair, went to Svāhā;
and the glorious six-faced one swiftly approached the Kṛttikās.
The son of the god of gods, the Lord, master of yogins,
fulfilled the desires of all at once with his forms.
Then Sambhu gave him the fourfold arsenal of weapons,
and Pārvatī [gave] a crest-jewel exuding drops of nectar.
Gaṅgā, her eyes blooming [with joy], gave Guha a single-stringed pearl necklace,
pure as her own mind, stainless, and born of nectar.
And the carrier of oblations gave to the capable son
a radiant, unfailing, and weighty spear that takes the lives of enemies.

blossomed, yellowed with its own pollen, and adorned with filaments.

to the charming peak of Mount Śveta, desiring to see the one whose banner is the bull.

Seeing all those denizens of heaven arrived there together,
Mahādeva welcomed them with a gracious [countenance].
Bowing to the lord of the god of gods and having obtained his leave,
the denizens of heaven of immeasurable splendour sat down on moon-white rocks.
Mount Śveta of lofty peaks, though already radiant,
became yet more radiant through the meeting of their splendours.
Then, urged by all the gods, the ruler of the gods,
the best of speakers, having bowed down, made representation to Mahādeva:
'O Lord, our fortune was forcibly seized by the one named Tāraka;
the thunderbolt was blunted upon his hard chest.
Hari’s blazing thousand-spoked discus of radiant power,
having reached that throat of the enemy of the gods, became soft.
The staff of the son of Vivasvat, glowing like kindled fire,
was extinguished upon the breast of that demon like a firebrand in a flood of water.

7.17.m:
The great noose of Pracetas, irresistible to foes in battle,
became upon his neck as if subdued by a spell.
Plucking up the wishing-trees by force in the Nandana [grove],
he planted them as he pleased in the grounds of his own household gardens.
In his presence the apprehensive wind acts like a palm-leaf fan;
fearful, the seasons attend upon him with heaps of their flowers.
While all the gods look on, O god of gods, this son of Diti
violently snatches away the sacrificial offering poured into the fire.

Having consecrated Skanda of great splendour as general,
the gods wish to conquer the king of the Daityas by your grace, O Śaṅkara.'
Thus petitioned there by the bearer of the thunderbolt, the one whose banner is the bull
gave permission to Skanda for the consecration to generalship.
Then, praised by hosts of gods, the one worthy of praise,
the destroyer of the body of Madana, having the crescent moon upon his crest,
gazing at his son with eyes blooming with affection,
instantly vanished into the mountain white as moonbeams.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, [entitled] 'Permission for the Consecration of Skanda'.

Sanatkumāra said:
Then, taking Skanda with them, those gods of immeasurable splendour,
led by Brahmā, came to the sacred Samantapañcaka.
On that bank of the Sarasvatī, sloping to the northeast, level,
spacious, free from holes, stones, thorns, and saline ground,
all those best of gods of the radiance of kindled fire
then sat down around Skanda with overjoyed minds.
That sacred place, joined with the immortals, became yet more sacred,
as the water of the Yamunā joined with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then the Earth in embodied form came to that region,
her eyes wide with joy as the consecration of Skanda took place.
Then that region quickly turned into golden sand,
variegated all around with the flashing rays of diverse jewels.

The region which those high-souled ones, free from malice, occupied / became free of sin through their splendour.
Then Himālaya, together with the [other] mountains, arrived, / taking a celestial, well-fashioned golden throne,
and taking golden pitchers filled with jewels, herbs, fragrances, / and holy waters, garlanded with blooming lotuses.
The oceans, highly agitated, their jewelled earrings swaying, / arrived there swiftly, their chests gleaming with pearl necklaces.

Having bright, well-adorned crystal pitchers brought, / filled with supremely holy waters and garlanded with rays of gems,

Under the pretext of an umbrella, Indra gave to that great-souled one / the complete fruit, as it were, of sovereignty over the gods. / Adorning the trees there with the abundant blossoming of flowers from the sky, / the seasons then arrived in that region with joyful hearts: / Arundhatī, Śacī, Svāhā, Sinīvālī, the daughter of the mountain king, / Aditi the mother of the gods, Night, Anumati, Kuhū, / Hrī, Śrī, Puṣṭi, the directions, and Heaven; all the daughters of Prajāpati; / Rākā, Dhiṣaṇā, Surabhi, and the wives of the gods; / the medicinal herbs in embodied form, the woodland deity, / the day, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, months, the year, and kalās.
Airāvaṇa, Supratīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, / Puṣpadanta, Mahāpadma, and Sārvabhauma—the elephants of the directions / brought everything required for the consecration of the great-souled one.
Tying up their matted locks, which shone like blazing fire, / the dwellers of the Himālayas, the best of sages, their power of austerity enhanced, joyfully approached the son of fire.

7.17.m:
Assembled together, their minds joyful and eager, the sons of the lotus-born [Brahmā] of great majesty, / bearing noble fame, approached the three-eyed god’s son whose preeminent power was rising. / Swiftly the lords of serpents approached, spreading awnings of rays from the jewels on their hoods; / even though venomous, they assumed exceedingly gentle forms, coming to the fire-born god of insurmountable valour. / And the Garuḍas, free of envy, their great strength well established over the king of serpents, / went very swiftly to him who was as lustrous as the young sun, the trees bent crooked by their wind-like speed. / With long and trembling eyes, endowed with diverse emotional gestures and charms, / endowed with the qualities of supreme youth and beauty, the delighted apsarases danced gracefully all around.
Tinged red with pollen of diverse flowers, carrying fragrant scents, / the breezes, free from dust, blowing very gently and pleasing to the minds of the gods, blew at that time.
Kindling the sacred fire properly, Bṛhaspati / performed the entire consecration rite for the reed-born god.

7.17.m:
Embracing the abode of blessings, the son of Śiva, / the sages then praised that praiseworthy one with foremost hymns of praise.
The Gandharvas and Nārada sang auspicious songs for him, / strumming the lute high, sweetly, and clearly.
Then, taking him by his right hand, having completed the auspicious rites, / the preceptor seated him upon that throne facing eastward. / Unbeaten, loud celestial drums of the gods / then sounded in the sky, exceedingly wondrous and completely captivating to the heart.
Various showers of flowers fell, accompanied by the humming of intoxicated bees, / bearing a reddish glow from their own filaments, and richly fragrant.
Praising Skanda with speeches from his four faces, Prajāpati [Brahmā] / first took up a vessel filled with sacred water.

7.17.m:
The Vasus too, their chests scarred by the tusks of the elephants of the enemies of the gods' lord, / took up vessels there filled with sacred water. / The two Aśvins also, fully adorned, took up two golden jars / filled with sacred waters, garlanded with jewel-rays. / The blazing fires, flaming with light, took up jars / covered with golden lotuses, variegated with jewel-beams. / The serpent and Gandharva kings, the world-guardians, the hosts of Maruts, / the seers, the Bālakhilyas, the ancestors, the lords of birds, / Dharma, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Kāla, Mṛtyu, and the Earth, / Sandhyā, Kānti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
the oceans, rivers, Vedas, sacred fords, mountains, and planets / took up jars there filled with supreme water. / Then, with delighted hearts, all of them consecrated / the exceedingly radiant, rejoiced son of the fire-god to the supreme command of the army. / Then all the sky-dwellers and the assembled seers together / raised a cry of victory for the victorious son of Śarva.

The daughter of the Himavat placed on the head of her son / a divine diadem arisen from nectar, presented by Pracetas. / On his broad chest, fair as gold, the best of rivers [Gaṅgā] / fastened a necklace with the luster of moonbeams. / 'Was the chest adorned by the necklace, or the necklace by Guha's chest?' / Such was the speculation that arose in the assembly of the gods. / Well-adorned Arundhatī fastened armlets / on the mighty-armed one's arms, thick as elephant tie-posts.
The radiant son of the fire-god then became even more radiant, / like a fire blazing at a sacrifice when ghee is offered into it.
Delighted, the four-faced lord [Brahmā] gave to that great soul / heroic, mighty attendants capable of changing their form at will: / Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Suraktākṣa, unconquerable Nandiṣeṇa, / and a fourth, Kumudamālin, celebrated as the best of the mighty. / Sthāṇu gave a greatly heroic attendant, Kratu, / who, when the terrible battle concerning Tāraka commenced,

And the Ocean then gave Saṃgraha and Vigraha, / holders of maces, two great attendants, to Kārttikeya. ||84|| / Pārvatī gave to her son Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, / and Śaṅkukarṇa hard to conquer, of great prowess and mighty power. ||85

7.17.m: Wearing diverse ornaments, with diverse garlands and unguents, / wearing diverse garments and likewise bearing diverse weapons, 177 / Kauśikī, overjoyed, gave these and others to Skanda. / Viṣṇu gave him the Vaijayantī garland with curved filaments, 178 / rich with various fragrances, fully blossomed and beautiful to behold, / and two spotless garments radiant as the morning sun. 179 / Joyful Pārvatī gave [them] to Skanda, whose mind was pleased. / Gaṅgā, glad at heart, gave Kumāra a water jar 180 / filled with water of nectar, produced from ambrosia, to the profound-minded one. / Garuḍa, well-pleased, gave his beloved son, 181 / a crested peacock with bright plumage, strong and shape-shifting, to Skanda. / Aruṇa gave a heroic red-crested cock, armed with talons, 182 / endowed with the power and speed of Śiva, pleasant to look upon, to Skanda. / Varuṇa gave a most powerful goat to Skanda, 183 / capable of bearing great burdens, moving where it willed, and changing form at will. / To the friend of brahmins Brahmā gave a pure black antelope skin garment 184 / resembling the belly of an eye agitated by a woman's amorous gestures. / Bṛhaspati, exceedingly pleased, gave a staff to that treasure of splendors, 185 / and a lovely garland of fine gold to Skanda.

7.17.m: Sanatkumāra said: / Placing Skanda at their head, all the gods quickly mobilized the army, / forcefully beating kettle-drums by the hundreds with large sticks decorated with gold and jewels. 1 . / Bringing the directional elephants that resembled mountain peaks, their limbs bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī, / the commanders of the army honored them with diverse perfumes and garlands. 2 . / Then, with supreme effort, having girded their flanks, they tied diverse armors / upon them carefully; on the chief elephants and horses [they fastened] golden equipment and weapons. 3 . / Bright banners and flags with beautiful golden poles were raised high; / they fastened various sets of razor-sharp darts and attached bells to their flanks. 4 . / And they harnessed the chariot, which had wheels of fine gold, made ready for battle, gleaming with rays of gems, / to swift flying horses with noble trappings and joyous hearts. 5 . / Śakra tied on an invaluable, completely clear armor, fair as the interior of a lotus, / ablaze with the light of the thunderbolt's radiance, upon his impenetrable chest anointed with yellow sandalwood. 6 . / Tying up their tawny, large matted locks high with hissing serpents, / the Rudras, delighted, [fastened] diverse armors upon their chests scarred by Daitya elephants. 7 . / Donning a bright armor, exceedingly radiant, with a sword fastened and wearing finger-guards, / holding a strung bow, his manly power blazing, the Moon did not abandon his innate gentleness. 8 . / [Apparatus readings]

7.17.m: The Lord of Wealth too, his arms thick as iron bars, directing his gaze, tawny as fire, / upon his mace, [contemplated] the destruction in slaughtering the enemies of the gods, either by the Lord's grace or by his own prowess. / Then, upon the army of the gods' enemies, huge meteors fell, flickering with sparks of fire; / without clouds the sky thundered terribly, and the earth with its trees and mountains trembled. / Dust raised by the wind fell down from the sky all around, grayish like a donkey's back; / banners with stout golden poles crashed down, and clouds released rains of blood. / Again and again, filled with dejection, horses shed lukewarm tears; / and the rut, dark blue like a pigeon's throat, deserted the broad temples of the elephants. / In flaming directions flocks of birds, beasts, and horses cried out loudly with distressed calls; / crushing rows of palaces all around, a violent wind blew fiercely.

7.17.m:
Weapons hurled against each other's armored bodies in combat / by the Daityas and immortals produced noise accompanied by flashing sparks of fire. / Seeing the Asuras endowed with strength and courage, some gods, without looking for allies, / rushed [against them] like bull elephants with dark temple areas due to streams of rut against rutting elephants.
The vanguard forces of the gods and Asuras, charging swiftly across the distance / and abandoning hope for their own lives, slew one another, displaying their manly valor. / Between them, whose minds harbored relentless hostility and who sought to slay one another, / there ensued a tumultuous clash, endless among the gods and Asuras in the great battle. / Elephants broke down pierced by javelins and lances; horses fell struck down by arrows; / and vomiting frothy blood from their mouths, warriors lost consciousness under severe blows.

7.17.m:
Severed by sharp crescent-shaped arrows, lotus-like faces adorned with earrings fell, / as the leaders of the Dānavas and gods manifested their pride and wrath to one another in the great combat. / Those Mothers and those Gaṇas ranged about, crushing the host of foes in battle / with blows of their fists, strikes with palms and heels, and by dragging, wrapping around, and crushing— / - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
The Gaṇas slew in battle the chief elephants of the Dānavas with rutting tuskers, / their best steeds with horses, their chariots with chariots, and their infantry troops with foot soldiers.
Leaping up swiftly with arrows, the leaders of the Gaṇas [struck] the warriors of the Daitya lord mounted on elephants, / their brains smashed and eyes knocked out by fist-blows and terrible strikes like thunderbolts.
Filled with rage, they hewed [them] with battle-axes, cut [them] with swords, and pierced [them] with tridents, / and crushed their foes with arms as stout as the tying-posts of mighty elephants.

7.17.m:
Then, seeing his forces violently slaughtered by the leaders of the Gaṇas, Tāraka, / his long eyes flushed with deep crimson rage, advanced, guarded by his elite royal forces.
Drawing his bow, which resounded like Indra's thunderbolt and blazed with the luster of gems, / he covered the vault of the sky with sheets of arrows tipped with heron and peacock feathers that pierced vital organs.
Learning of the arrival of that lord of Daityas from his shouts, the Son of Fire, gazing up / at the spear resting in his hand, adorned with delightful bells of exquisite gold— / that roar of Kārttikeya, piercing the sky and the cardinal and intermediate directions, / then violently bewildered the minds of the gods' enemies in the great encounter.

7.17.m: Then, seeing Tāraka rushing forward, protected by a mighty force in the great battle, / Guha hurled his spear, shining like kindled fire, for the destruction of the enemies of the gods. / Hurled by that son of Fire, covering the sky and the directions with its flames, / it multiplied manifold in the firmament, terrible, bewildering the Daityas like an illusion. / And it fell upon the armored chests of the enemies of the gods who wore variegated mail; / moving with irresistible speed among them all, it cleaved their chests and quickly entered within. / Struck by it, all those enemies of the gods, their wide, large eyes rolling and red, / their tongues and lower lips bitten, their limbs convulsing, vomited blood and gave up their lives. / Just as the sun shatters the unabating darkness equally with its rays, / so the son of Fire tore apart the armies of his enemies on the battlefield with his spears. / Having slain all the enemies of the gods of exalted pride and prowess on the battlefield, / the spear then returned to Skanda, just as radiance [returns to] the sun after scorching the worlds.

7.17.m: Vyāsa said: / O lord, knower of all righteousness, endowed with the power of great yoga, / I have heard all this great deed of Skanda. / From you, O supreme master of yoga, [I have heard] the highest secret of the Lord. / What further did the lord of gods, the enemy of Tripura who bears the bull upon his banner, do / after sending Guha, the great commander of the army, together with the gods, / and entrusting the deities to Skanda? / And where did the lord of gods go? What did the Daughter of the Mountain say? / And what things did Umā say to him? Relate this to me who am asking. / Sūta said: / Thus questioned then by Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā of great austerity, / who knows the supreme meaning of all scriptures, began to relate. / Sanatkumāra said: / Having entrusted the gods to the Six-Faced One, the god of gods, Bhava, then / went together with the goddess to Mandara, which possesses golden caves. / There he sat upon a great, radiant golden seat, / strewn with diverse gems, lofty like a golden peak. / At his side, the goddess, the daughter of the Himavat, shone, / like Rohiṇī standing near the full moon in a cloudless sky.

Because I protect the beasts (paśu) and create [them] at will, / and I am their lord (pati), therefore I am remembered as Paśupati. / I alone am the ruler (īśa) over others, and others do not rule over me, / and I lead my devotees to lordship; therefore I am proclaimed as Īśāna.
871 / For the directions are my garments; I dwell in all directions, / and I am the dwelling of the directions; therefore I am remembered as Digvāsas.
Because I am the bringer of auspiciousness (śaṅkara) to living beings, for that reason I am remembered as Śaṅkara. / Because I bring well-being (śiba) to the worlds, therefore I am remembered as Śiva. / Since [a portion] of my body is blue (nīla) and tinged with a red (lohita) lustre, / for that reason I am proclaimed as Nīlalohita.'

"Śūlī" is proclaimed because of the trident (śūla), and "Lākulī" because of the club (lakula). / When one chants "Rudra", O goddess, the fruit is regarded as that of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
When one utters "Hara", one obtains the fruit of a Gosava sacrifice; / and when one chants "Bhava", one is instantly freed from all sins.
[Chanting] "Puruṣa" [yields] supreme happiness, and "Aja" [yields] residence in the same world [with him]; / "Īśāna" [yields] great sovereignty, and "Mahādeva" [yields] imperishable [reward].
[Chanting] "Digvāsas" [yields] supreme liberation, "Śaṅkara" great joy, / "Śiva" utmost auspiciousness, and "Śūlī" supreme strength.
By chanting "Lākulī", a man attains higher realms; / chanting "Nīlalohita", my devotee obtains the fruits of all sacrifices in this world,
O goddess, and an imperishable dwelling in me. / Thus, O Vyāsa, the explanation of the meanings of the names has been related

Sanatkumāra said: / "Listen, dear child, to how rebirth was given by the Pināka-bearer / to Śveta, whose lifespan was exhausted, as he was being seized by Yama.
There was a sage named Darbhadhvaja, equal to Bṛhaspati, / whose son, Kuśadhvaja, was disciplined in all disciplines;
he became endowed with immense fiery radiance, like a second Viśvāmitra. / He had a dear son of great luster named Śveta.
From the very birth of that son of Kuśadhvaja, / devotion to the Bull-bannered [Lord] remained inseparable like a shadow.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, or performing austerities, / the great sage remained meditating with his whole being on the Lord of gods.
Then, in the course of time, O best of brahmins, a powerful Dānava named Vipṛthu / approached the father of Śveta and asked for his daughter [in marriage].
And he did not give that daughter to the enemy of the gods; / therefore he, and Darbhadhvaja as well, was forcibly slain at night by him.
For he, as well as his daughter, O virtuous one, / had desired the bearer of the discus and mace, the supremely righteous Viṣṇu, as a son-in-law.
Knowing that her father had been slain, his virtuous daughter, / observing great vows, went to [perform] austerities for the sake of the Supreme.
Śveta too, learning of that, took to supreme dispassion; / having reached the bank of the Narmadā, with a focused mind and subdued senses,
his state of mind surrendered to Rudra alone, devoted to him, intent on him, / the ascetic remained performing fierce austerities, steadfast in yoga.

7.17.m: Those mighty lords of the gaṇas, having received the command from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, / quickly went near the sage Śveta, as if wishing to burn up the messengers of Antaka. / Having arrived, they saw Śveta being tormented by the messengers of Yama, / like a single deer surrounded in the forest by many hunters, / bound around his neck by the noose of time, and bound by his hands and feet, / dragged by Mṛtyu himself, whose eyes were trickling with blood, / with deformed faces, large fangs, reddish-brown beards and hair, / with eyes resembling lightning, and fierce iron clubs in their hands, / being struck on all sides by the most terrifying messengers of Yama. / Having seen that sage thus afflicted, crying out aloud repeatedly, "O Lord!", the leader of the gaṇas / quickly released the sage from the noose, as the Lord frees beasts from their bond. / "Depart, servants of Yama, having left the sage here with [your] firm bodies! / For he is devoted to the unborn Śambhu, the lord of gods and asuras, the cause of the universe. / He who is the creator of wind, fire, Indra, and the Maruts, praised by Brahmā and the others, / the undefeated one whose banner bears the lord of bulls, is his protector; Yama shall not look upon him!"

Release him; do not suffer weariness in vain! / For even if protected for a long time, he shall indeed come to me alone. / In this world, no one whose lifespan is exhausted when their time has expired, / even if endowed with austerity and virtue, even if learned, can remain alive. / Whatever deed, virtuous or censured, has been performed by him, / O lords of the gaṇas, having abandoned this body, let him receive that! / The examination of all this multitude of living beings is dependent on me. / Thus the investigation of deeds, whether meritorious or sinful, [is mine]. / Therefore quickly deliver this Śveta to me, whose life has ended!

7.17.m: Nandī, the lord of all gaṇas, having bowed with supreme devotion / to Bhava of boundless splendour, related what had happened. / And having heard the word spoken by Nandī, the Lord / directly spoke to Vaivasvata in a gentle and deep voice: / "This Śveta has supreme devotion to Me, O lord of the host of spirits! / Therefore, even though his lifespan has ended, Mṛtyu shall have no power over him. / By his great austerity and devotion, his mind fixed in contemplation on Me, / Mṛtyu has been conquered by this Śveta through My grace, O tormentor! / By My command, no humiliation of him is to be done by you. / Do you not know, O son of the Sun, that the best of men devoted to Me / do not see your abode, even when dissolution of the body is at hand? / I am supremely pleased by his extraordinary devotion.

7.17.m:
He wards off the approach of those men who are evildoers.
Where yogins, gods, perfected beings, and supreme seers,
having bowed to him, attained perfection, the auspicious abode of Paśupati.
Simply by forming the resolve, 'I will behold Mahālaya,'
a living being is freed from actions termed grave sins.
Mahālaya is a great sacred field, auspicious, granting liberation and perfection;
by seeing it, a man saves seven generations on both sides of his lineage.
Next to that, O Vyāsa, is the exceedingly holy place named Kedāra,
the supreme, auspicious abode of the Bull-bannered One, to the north of that very spot.
There, on that best of mountains, the divine lord Hara himself,
it is said, released holy water from the mass of his matted locks, […]
[…] arose there, issuing from the crest of Hara.

7.17.m:
Endowed with magnificent forms, noble, possessing splendor exceeding even that of Nandin.
Having seen the God of gods, the Lord of the world, dwelling in Kedāra,
[…]
Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Soma, and the lord of the Yakṣa hordes
worship the Supreme Lord abiding there with devotion.
Those noble men by whom the water of Kedāra is drunk—
how could they lament, O Vyāsa? What joy have they not attained?
That water pouring down at Kedāra, on the crest of the mountain Himavat,
from the head of the all-pervading wielder of the trident, the creator of Soma, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts,
which those delighting in unrighteousness cannot obtain to drink without the grace of Śiva—
having drunk that, living beings are freed from the fearful bondage of worldly existence.
Here itself is Madhyameśvara, the primordial abode of the husband of Umā;
having gone to that lord of the gods as well, one attains the state of a gaṇa lord.

Where the Goddess performed austerity desiring a fair complexion;
it is renowned throughout the three worlds simply as Gaurīśikhara.
At the sacred ford known as Kucakuṇḍa, made there by Umā,
those men who go to that holy Gaurīśikhara,
Attaining the fruit of an horse sacrifice, they go to the supreme destination.
There is another peak, Ṛṣabha, resembling diamond and crystal,
Where Nandī performed austerity and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara.
Reaching that peak Ṛṣabha, the holy abode of the husband of Umā,
and beholding it, one is freed from sin and attains the world of Rudra.
There is yet another peak of the snow mountain, radiant like Hemakūṭa,
where there is the auspicious sanctuary of Rudra named Bhastreśvara;
Rudra is remembered as the god Bhastreśvara on that mountain.
Bowing to that Mahādeva, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as men terrified of death and tormented by the sorrows of birth,

Reaching that sanctuary, obtain their desires according to their wish.
Beholding it, a man gains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice, O Vyāsa.
At Gaṅgādvāra, the auspicious gateway of great holiness, a liṅga
was established by the noble Dakṣa out of devotion to the one with matted locks,
where trees made of gold were called Kanakhala;
due to the misconduct of humans, they became cut down and turned into [mere] timber.
Where Śambhu, the soul of the universe, the lord of the universe, along with Ambikā,
is named Bahurūpeśvara, granting boons to manifold living beings.
Men who desire liberation do not behold rebirth […];
beholding him, a man obtains ten times the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
885
Beholding which Īśvara, whose throat is like a dark raincloud,
hosts of gods, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas, and Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Dānavas,
do not fall again into the mire of worldly existence.

Those men who reach that Japyeśvara and give up their vital breaths / will be freed from birth and death and dwell in the abode of Śiva.
There is another sanctuary, O Vyāsa, of the one whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon, / which is renowned in the world, O sage, as Mahābhairava.

There the trident-bearing god, the bull-bannered one himself, / assumed a terrifying form that frightened Nandin, Umā, and the gaṇas;
seeing which, the daughter of the Himavat became overwhelmed with fear. / There, having terrified the mountain's daughter for the sake of sport,
Bhava again assumed a gentle form and comforted the daughter of the mountain. / Therefore that sanctuary is called Mahābhairava.
Approaching Bhairaveśvara, he who sees the Pināka-bearer, / O Vyāsa, will never again suffer death and birth.
Whatever merit belongs to those in the orders of life, and likewise to those who observe vows to the Lord, / that fruit the best among men obtains upon seeing Bhairava.
Kumbhakāreśvara as well, and likewise Utkuṭukeśvara, / and also Chagalaṇḍeśvara are places arisen from Mahābhairava.
By seeing these three places, one becomes a sovereign of the three worlds. / Another sanctuary of Śiva is also spoken of, named Rudrakoṭi.

7.17.m:
For the sake of alms, the trident-holder indeed entered that forest. / There that Lord of gods was seen by the sages with an erect penis.
Out of jealousy, the great liṅga of that god / was made to fall by the deluded sages in the hermitage of the Devadāru forest, O Vyāsa.
When that liṅga fell down, the world became devoid of sexual marks; / all that is immovable and movable appeared neuter.
Then the gods headed by Brahmā and those Siddhas desirous of liberation, / knowing all that dreadful destruction to have arisen from Śaṅkara,
praised Śaṅkara with various hymns and fully satisfied him. / Then that liṅga of the Pināka-bearer became just as it was before,
and straightaway masculine virility returned to the world. / There a liṅga of the Supreme Lord was installed by them with devotion.
Having seen it, one obtains the fruit of ten horse sacrifices. / Thus, O great sage, exists this sacred Dāru forest of the Lord.

Another auspicious sanctuary of Bhava is known by the name Uktaratha, / which is auspicious and always frequented by gods, kinnaras, and gandharvas. (102) / There stands the mountain named Śrīparvata, the abode of fortune, / that supreme sacred field of perfection, crowded with hundreds of siddhas and immortals. (103)
Where a thousand holy liṅgas of the Trident-Holder, which grant boons, / were installed, O Vyāsa, by the noble-minded Śilāda. (104)
Those men who behold that Īśāna residing on Śrīparvata / never have any fear of birth and death. (105) / In this very body, in that sacred field whose essence is Bhava, / brahmins devoted to the practice of yoga attain their desired perfection. (106) / Those men who visit Śrīgiri even in their minds, O sage, / do not go to the abode of Yama even when death arrives. (107)

Then there is Northern Gokarṇa, an hermitage marked by the liṅga of Hara, / where fierce austerity was performed by flesh-eating rākṣasas. (108) / The desired boon was obtained by noble ones beginning with Rāvaṇa; / where previously, having performed austerity and pleased the Pināka-bearer, (109) / Rāvaṇa attained universal sovereignty over the three worlds. / Having seen it, a man obtains tenfold the fruit of a horse sacrifice, (110) / and when he dies he goes to sayūjya with Rudra; of this there is no doubt. / Next is Southern Gokarṇa, the holy place of the Pināka-bearer, (111)
where, with the spṛkkā grown on the ridges of Laṅkā and Malaya, / the blessed god, the lord of the chiefs of all immortals, is worshipped. (112) / Where even today that foremost rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa alone, / having worshipped the lord of immortals, enjoys his kingdom free from anxiety. (113)

The men who visit the hermitage and sanctuary of Gokarṇa / obtain the auspicious fruit of ten horse sacrifices. (114) / There is the mountain known as Hariścandra, possessing many cascades, / upon which a sanctuary was built by Rāma, son of Jamadagni. (115)
Where gods, siddhas, yakṣas, guhyakas, and kinnaras, / as well as vow-observers and yogins, bowed to the Bull-bannered One. (116) / Those by whom the summit of Mount Hariścandra has been seen up to its peak / do not dwell among mortals, having become gods again, O sage. (117)

7.17.m:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, at a distance of one yojana along the road, / is the great sanctuary of the Three-eyed One, the place called Kārohaṇa, (118) / where Prajāpati mounted a crow who was practicing austerities. / Because Prajāpati mounted a crow in that place, (119) / for that reason that place is celebrated by the name Kārohaṇa. / And in that place the blessed Bull-bannered Lord descended. (120)
Understand why that land is holier than all lands: / when the Kṛtayuga had waned, O Vyāsa, at the dawn of the Tretāyuga, (121)
Dharma, oppressed by adharma, cast off one foot upon it; / a second when the Dvāpara arrived, and a third in the Kaliyuga. (122)
And with the fourth he remained standing, since the blessed Lord was there; / thus, because of the cohabitation of Dharma, that land is considered most holy. (123)
Becoming Bhārabhūti in that land, the Pināka-bearer, / having bound the burdens of the twice-born, cast them into the Narmadā. (124)

7.17.m: And in the Dvāpara, becoming Āṣāḍhi, he bestowed grace through dance. / In this way, in each yuga in that land, O Vyāsa, Śiva himself (126) / descended and bestowed grace upon the pure-minded brahmins. / Whoever has seen all the sanctuaries of that god, O man of good vows, / would attain the world of Īśāna. / And knowing the world to be tormented by suffering in the present Kali age, (128) / having created four persons from his four faces, / the Supreme Lord spoke, wishing to bestow favor on the world: (129) / 'All of you go to earth, having become twice-born ascetics; / after leading the brahmins to the supreme abode, you yoga-lords shall come to me.' (130) / Having been spoken to thus, O Vyāsa, they then came into being separately / among human beings as brahmins devoted to the dharma of liberation. (131) / In Ujjayinī, the eldest teacher named Kauśika by name; / the second indeed as Gārgya in Jambūmārga, full of tapas; (132) / and the third, the high-minded Mitra, was in Mathurā; / while the fourth, a brahmacārin of noble lineage, was among the Kurus. (133) / And the blessed Lord of gods, united with Amareśvara, / [was born to] the one named Somaśarman, born in the lineage of Atri. (134)

Lākulī imparted the yoga of his own established doctrine and said this: / 'Indeed, this is the supreme secret known as the Pañcārtha. / It has been given to you to liberate brahmins from mortal bondage. / By means of this initiation, bring brahmins to the supreme state.
On holy riverbanks, in sacred shrines, / in abandoned houses, and in forests—there shall be your dwelling, free from attachment.' / Hearing the words of the Blessed One, the disciples of Paśupati, / possessing the splendor of Bhava, all did as they were instructed.
Because Bhava descended in the land marked by the foot of Dharma, / that region is considered supreme, most exceptionally sacred.

Where the sin-destroying hermitage of yogins was established, / that abode of the great-souled one is known as Aṣṭāyatana. / Seeing it, O Vyāsa, men attain the supreme state. / The human beings who approach Kārohaṇa, the dwelling place of Śiva, / have no fear of lying in a womb, O best of sages. / The expanse between the Mahī and the Narmadā, and the interior of the Sahya,
is this ancient sacred field of Paśupati, praised by seers. / Coming there, O Vyāsa, even if a man has committed great sins, / freed from all sins, he attains the destination he desires.

7.17.m:
Kārohaṇa is an exceedingly holy place where Śaiva shrines reside, O wise one; / having gone to those shrines of great fruit, men do not enter the house of saṃsāra again.
There is also another holy shrine revered by the seven worlds / in Vārāṇasī, O best of sages, where Hara is perpetually present.
There, the sacred Bhāgīrathī flows toward the north; / it is a field of perfection, a vast sacred field renowned in the three worlds. / It is known by name as Avimukta ('never forsaken'), for it is never forsaken by Hara. / Beholding the god Avimukteśvara there, the husband of Umā,
the state of gaṇas is declared [for a person] at the time of death, O great sage. / Where the mighty Vidyutkeśa, lord of gaṇas, stands at the gate,
along with Daṇḍapāṇi of great splendor, by the command of the Self-manifest One. / Without seeing him, they do not see Hara, the lord of the god of gods, / even yogins of great soul; darśana of him is also meritorious. / When a pure person sees Daṇḍapāṇi, the gaṇa upon whom Hara bestowed boons,

Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere when a liṅga of Śambhu is established, / that is declared to be a thousandfold when it is set up in Avimukta.
Whether a woman or a man establishes one according to rule and precedent, / a thousand liṅgas of the Lord are considered established by that person.
Three-eyed, becoming a lord of gaṇas, he goes to union with Rudra. / For this reason, O best of sages, by the gods led by Brahmā and the Sun,
liṅgas were established there by all the foremost gods. / In that sacred field of the Lord, in the city of Kāśī, in many places,
liṅgas established by great souls are seen even today. / Through the remembrance of Avimukta, even if one is situated at the edge of the earth,
a creature is freed from sins, and having died, obtains bliss.

7.17.m:
Brahmins who know the truth and meaning of the Veda shed [their bodies] there, / as do siddhas and Pāśupatas who desire liberation from the bond of existence.
Having reached auspicious Vārāṇasī, the unsurpassed sacred field of perfections, / what creature would have the thought of departing elsewhere again?
That sacred field of the moon-crested [Lord] is praised in the Vedas, O Vyāsa, / as granting the state of perfection and liberation to the embodied being who gives up his vital breaths.
Those men devoted to Rudra who dwell in Avimukta / dwell in the abode of Rudra, O Vyāsa; of this there is no doubt.
Standing, walking, sleeping, eating, performing work, or even laughing, / whatever embodied soul remembers Avimukta, whence can there be fear of rebirth for him?
There is no sacred field higher than Avimukta; there is no realm higher than Avimukta; / there is no merit higher than Avimukta; there is no destination higher than Avimukta.

This holy [abode] of Umā's husband, resorted to by the foremost gods for perfection, / is known as Avimukta, attended by Brahmā and the rest for peace; / mortals supremely devoted to the Lord who resort to it to attain serenity, / freed from the dread arising from existence, attain supreme liberation.
And at Prayāga, the sacred field of austerity, there is a great shrine of the God; / having seen it properly, a man attains his desired destination.

7.17.m:
At Naimiṣa there is a great shrine of Rudra, the God of gods; / having seen it, completely freed from sin, one attains the heavenly world.
In Kurukṣetra, the sacred field of dharma, there is the great abode of Yogeśvara; / when that is seen, O foremost of brahmins, one attains leadership of the gaṇas.
And when he dies, he attains the world of Rudra, where all desires are fulfilled. / At Gayā there is another auspicious abode of the blessed Lord,
named Gadhrakūṭeśvara, which releases from all sins; / having seen it, the foremost among men are not bewildered at the time of death.
Having smeared ashes there, one is freed from all sins, / and a twice-born obtains the fruit of even a twelve-year vow.

7.17.m:
In Magadha there is another sacred shrine of the bearer of the Pināka, / in the city of Pāṭalīputra, named Prahasiteśvara.
Approaching that Lord, one obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice. / Eight abodes of the moon-crested Lord are recorded in Magadha,
which Nakulīśvara, surrounded by disciples, wandered through; / having seen them, a man is immediately freed from sin.
Among the Yavanas another sacred abode of Umā's husband is recorded; / having seen that Lord, a mortal attains heaven.

895
In the country of Aṅga, a supremely holy abode of the bearer of the Pināka is declared, / named Hemacūḍeśvara; having seen it, one is not bewildered.
Then, O Vyāsa, at the confluence of the Bhāgīrathī and the ocean, / there is a holy liṅga of the bearer of the Pināka established by Brahmā.
Just by approaching it, one is freed from all sins; / having seen it, one obtains the fruit of ten horse sacrifices.
Having seen the trident-bearer at Prabhāsa, at the dissolution of the body one becomes a gaṇa. / Having seen Śaṅkara at Puṣkara, one does not grieve over death and birth.
And on Mahendra, the foremost of mountains, there is an auspicious shrine of Rudra; / approaching it, a wise man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Approaching the god Mahākāleśvara in Ujjayinī, a wise man / of great vows obtains the status of a gaṇa of the enemy of Tripura.
Having seen the god Drimicaṇḍeśvara, a man saves / seven generations on both sides and attains [the merit of] all sacrifices.

Having seen Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, a man does not grieve over death. / Likewise, on the peak of the snow mountain, resorted to by siddhas and kinnaras,
there is the great shrine of Rudra known as Ḍiṅgeśvara. / Having approached and seen that God, the Lord of the universe,
devoted to the worship of Śiva, O Vyāsa, one obtains all desires; / and for that great-souled one when dead, the destination declared is leadership of the gaṇas.
At Suvarṇākṣa is recorded a supreme abode of the God of gods; / having seen it, O Vyāsa, a man obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice.

896 / Another most holy and excellent abode is celebrated in the world, / renowned by the name Bhadreśvara, frequented by gods and gandharvas. (197) / Beholding it, O Vyāsa, a mortal obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. / Whatever great inauspicious deed has been done since birth (198) / is entirely destroyed that very moment upon seeing Hara as Bhadreśvara. / And wherever he dies, a man obtains the status of a gaṇa. (199)
Blessed are those mortals, O Vyāsa, devoted to Rudra and endowed with great splendor, / who behold Bhadreśa, who dispels the fear of birth and death. (200) / Having seen the abode of the omnipresent Lord at Ekāmra, one attains heaven; / having seen Hara at Virajā, one obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice. (201) / Having seen the Lord of gods, Paśupati the sovereign, in Nepāla, / one obtains [the fruit of] ten horse sacrifices and goes to the realm of Rudra. (202) / Attaining the dissolution of the body, one is liberated from bestiality. / There is another abode on the Snow Mountain, Naikatuṅgādhipeśvara. (203)

Having seen it, O best of sages, a mortal is not born again. / It is declared to bestow all desires upon devotees who bow [there]. (204)
Thus these holy abodes of Rudra have been recounted to you / by me, O Vyāsa, by which an auspicious destination is attained. (205)
Whatever brahmin, restrained in self, recites these day by day, / to him the bull-bannered god grants union with himself. (206)
A pure man should constantly perform the recitation of Śambhu's abodes, / which brings good fortune, is supremely holy, pure, and dispels all fear. (207)

Thus, this residence in the world of the bearer of the daughter of the best of mountains, Viṣṇu, and the Gaṅgā, / granting all desires, has been taught to you by the son of the best of sages, purifying [one] of sin. / Speak, O Vyāsa, what else may I tell you? (208)
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the description of the abodes of Śiva.

7.17.m:
Sūta said: / Having heard the story concerning the abodes of the one whose diadem bears the crescent moon, / the sage Vyāsa spoke these words to the son of Brahmā, the knower of Brahman, the lord among sages: (1) / 'O Venerable One, this righteous, most holy, and secret account has been taught to me by you according to rule. / What other seer could know thus the cherished abodes of Śambhu? (2) / I wish to know how Tripura was burnt in former times with a single arrow / by the wielder of the divine Pināka, bestower of boons on devotees; tell me that as it happened, O sage.' (3) / Thus questioned by the sage, the lord among sages answered the inquiry duly, / saying these words: 'Hear, my son, how that Tripura was burnt. (4) / When that lion of bull-like leaders among daityas, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, a great hero, was slain in former times / and the daityas and dānavas were broken, Maya was distressed with impatience and grief. (5) / Abandoned by the sovereignty of the kings of dānavas, he, the artisan of the universe, became like the god with the makara banner bereft of Rati. / Taking the daitya Tārakākṣa, and Vidyutprabha of splendor equal to Indra, (6) / he performed fierce austerity, an agent of vast deeds, and those two daityas, whose strength was equal to Andhaka. / In the cold season, standing on the snow mountain, and in summer, scorched by five fires, (7) / and in the rainy season, in the cloudless sky over ground flooded with water, they performed austerity with great effort. / A thousand divine years passed for them as they remained in such extremely fierce austerity. (8)

Then Maya, utterly confounded, spoke these words: "Let the boon remain as I requested!

At that moment, when the three divine cities are joined together, O hero among gods, ..
he who can burn that Tripura with a single arrow—let him be the destroyer of our Tripura!"
Having heard those words of Maya, Brahmā, delighted in his inner self,
granted that desired boon to the lord of the Danujas, and having granted it, went swiftly to his own city. ..
Then Maya fashioned that Tripura, like the creator of the world in the beginning of a cosmic age.
He made the first [city] out of iron; then the next out of silver, like a mountain; ..

Then, filled with wrath against Maya, all the rulers of the dwellers of heaven assembled together
and swiftly reported the whole matter in full to the Grandfather.
Comforting all the lords of the gods, the god seated on the lotus throne said to them:
"Those supreme Asuras of Tripura are exceedingly mighty; indeed, they cannot be slain by you by force.
Therefore, taking you with us, Viṣṇu and I shall go to Śambhu for refuge.
The moon-bearer is always our recourse, O lords of the gods; he who holds the trident in hand shall slay them by his might." ..
Saying "So be it," those gods—Brahmā, the Sun, Śakra, the Wind, Fire, and the others—bowed down,
went to Kailāsa, beheld Hara, the lord of the lords of gods, and praised him reverently to achieve their goal:
"Homage to the one venerated by the lord of the three worlds, who holds the earth dear, of boundless valor!
Homage to the one whose crest is illuminated by the radiant splendor of the crescent moon on his mass of matted hair!
Homage forever to the god of the three worlds; homage likewise to the bearer of the Pināka bow!
Homage to the one who has a blazing sword and axe; homage forever to the one who holds a trident in his hand! ..

7.17.m:
The gods said:
“O Lord, by the three dānavas, Maya and the others, who obtained boons granted by Brahmā, / Tripura has been made an impenetrable fortress, and we are harassed by [those] arrogant in their strength. // 1
All the apsarases have been abducted, and the groves have been destroyed. / And they said: ‘Today we kill all the gods; tomorrow we shall kill [them all].’ // 2
Even this grandfather Brahmā is not able to restrain them, / nor is Viṣṇu, O Mahādeva! Because of that, great fear is upon us. // 3
Therefore, best of gods, act in such a way that Tripura may be destroyed and they may be slain; / let this boon be granted to us.” // 4
Having been thus petitioned by all those foremost of the gods, / Śambhu of great splendor said this, as if reassuring the gods: // 5
“Taking a hundredth portion of my splendor, O lords of the gods, / and becoming embodied with the splendor of Rudra, you shall slay the dānavas.” // 6

Then the gods spoke these words once more to the lord: / “We are not able to bear even a thousandth part of yours. // 7

7.17.m:
Then the blessed God, whose banner bears a bull, / reassuring the anxious dwellers of heaven who were bowed low, said again: // 13
“If it is so, O lions among gods, by discharging a single arrow at once / in the moment of a twinkling of an eye, I shall burn that great, impenetrable Tripura. // 14
For the pleasure of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and for the favor of Śakra, / mounting a chariot, I myself shall destroy that Tripura.” // 15
"Let that chariot be prepared, mounting which, O gods, / I will burn the impregnable Tripura occupied by the three Dānavas. / And of such a nature that it can bear me, O foremost among the gods, / mighty and like the Himavat—such a chariot must be made."
Then the gods, having bowed to the Lord, became delighted in their minds, / and coming together, all of them fashioned an excellent chariot. / Then the venerable Brahmā, along with Viṣṇu and the Fire-god, / made that excellent, divine chariot consisting of all the gods.

Dhātṛ, the Sun, Śakra, the Wind, the Lord of Wealth, Yama, / the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas, the Gandharvas, and the two Aśvins;
the Garuḍas, mountains, Nāgas, Guhyakas, along with the great oceans, / the seers, Siddhas, and Yakṣas, planets […]

they arranged those eight orders of gods into that chariot. / Some they placed in the two wheels, splendour […] / […] and other foremost gods they yoked to the chariot. / Having made the four Vedas into horses, they yoked them to that chariot.

7.17.m: Then the venerable Śambhu, being praised by the three gods, / looked upon the divine chariot made of all the gods. / Saying, "Well made! Excellent!", he took up that great bow. / Grasping that blazing, supreme bow filled with all brilliance, / looking below and above, the Lord of the Universe was pleased. / Then, looking at the Grandfather, the Lord of Speech said: / "O Brahman, this chariot and this bow have been well fashioned by you; / bring quickly the arrow by which Tripura must be burned!" / Then Brahmā, having bowed to the bull-bannered [god], said to him: / "This chariot, O God, and this bow have been made by me for you. / Only the Lord Himself is able to make that arrow suitable for it." / Then, seeing Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and the Fire-god standing at his side, / the tamer of foes summoned those two gods with a glance. / Both of them, with folded hands, presented themselves before the Lord of the gods. / Then Śambhu himself fashioned Viṣṇu into the best of arrows; / he joined Soma, the lord of medicinal plants, to its feather-socket, / and made Agni its tip. Then he said to Brahmā: / "O Brahman, who has been designated by you here as the charioteer for the chariot?" / Then Brahmā, with folded hands, said to the Lord of the World: / "If you give me the command, I myself shall be the charioteer.

7.17.m: This venerable Lord who is the Lord of the lords of all beings, / the creator and destroyer of us and of the deities—he is the sovereign. .70. / He comes in person to destroy; what expedient could work for him? / Bowing down and taking refuge are the two virtuous expedients with the wearer of matted hair; .71. / these two are to be employed in appeasing him: such is my opinion. / If, adopting stubbornness, we fight Pinākin, .72. / by his crooked glance alone we asuras are slain. / Brahmā and the others, when afflicted, go to Śambhu for refuge, for the sake of peace. .73. / When one is attacked by him in person, who could be his refuge? / To whom belongs this entire manifest world, O daityas, beginning with Brahmā, .74.

7.17.m:
How is it that, being sons of Danu, kings proud of your strength, / you wish to conquer death out of fear, like wretched beings, O Dānavas?
If you surrender your lives in battle, you will attain greater sovereignty; / if you perish without a fight, an inauspicious destination will be yours.
Moreover, if you are slain by the god of gods, the trident-bearer, / you will without doubt become lords of the Pramathas thereafter.

7.17.m:
There is no benefit in entering into an alliance with the gods. / Your resolve for war is proper, and it is manifest, and we are yours.
Pleased with your valour, the bull-bannered god might perhaps / grant you a boon, O Daityas; therefore, heroic prowess is better for you.
And I shall create for you a protective amulet that fends off the blows of weapons. / Arise, sons of Danu, with a desire to fight for victory!"
Having heard the words of Nārada, the mighty Tārakākṣa, / Vidyunmālin, and the other chief Daityas, along with Bāṇa and the other great asuras—
oppressed by the noose of Time, deluded, their merit exhausted, their lifespans ended— / said: "This has been spoken well and excellently by Nārada."
Maya too, perceiving those words and knowing that destruction was at hand, / indeed spoke these words: "What Nārada has said is excellent."

7.17.m:
Nārada then, delighted, bound the amulet by magical power; / having made the asuras eager to fight, he went toward Śarva's chariot.
Then all those Dānavas, resolved upon battle, / equipped with diverse weapons, became eager for combat.
Tārakākṣa, Bala, Bāṇa, and the Dānava Vidyunmālin, / all the kings, having donned their armour together, stood in the forefront.
Then conches and thousands of trumpets were sounded / in the terrible army of the Dānavas, causing dread to cowards.
"That chariot is coming here; another one is seen over there! / How did it arrive?" In this manner they spoke words to one another.

चण्डेश्वरश्चण्डवपुर्महात्मा ज्वलत्प्रदीप्तोग्रकुठारपाणिः .
व्यादाय वक्त्रं पुरतः स्थितोभूद् देवस्य शम्भोः प्रमथेन्द्रवीरः ..3 . .
दीप्तं त्रिशूलं परिगृह्य नन्दी त्र्यक्षः प्रतस्थे4 हरतुल्यवर्ष्मा5 .
पार्श्वे स्थितोभूत् स च शंकुकर्णः प्रगृह्य दीप्तं मुशलं गजेन्द्रः . .4..

वज्रत्रिशूलासिभुशुण्डिहस्ता युयुत्सवस्तस्थुरुपेतहर्षाः . .5. .
समागतं तं रथमीक्ष्य6 दैत्या युद्धाय निर्जग्मुरुपेतमोहाः .
ते तारकाक्षप्रमुखाः सुवीरा सन्नह्य नानायुधदीप्तहस्ताः . .6. .
सार्धं गणेन्द्रैः समरं प्रचक्रुर्दनोः सुताः कोपवशं प्रयाताः .
देवोपि चन्द्रार्धनिकेतमौलिः7 शरं न चिक्षेप पुरं प्रदग्धुम् ..7..
तस्थौ तथैवा8सकृदात्मना च पश्यन् रणं तद्गणदैत्यपानाम् .
ततः स नन्दी गणपैः प्रवीरैरचीकरद्युद्धमदीनसत्वैः . .8. .

7.17.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that chariot approached that Tripura situated at the head of the western ocean, / having a radiant, multi-coloured crest with various banners, like Mount Meru, king of mountains, of golden stone.
Seeing the fortress of Tripura, those lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandīśa and Caṇḍīśa, well-prepared, / together raised a roar, those great warriors eager to fight with the lion-like lords of the Dānavas.
Caṇḍeśvara of fierce form, the magnanimous one, with a blazing, burning, terrible axe in hand, / opening his mouth wide, stood before the god Śambhu, a hero among the lords of the Pramathas.
Grasping a blazing trident, the three-eyed Nandī, equal in body to Hara, stood firm; / and at his side stood the lord of elephants, Śaṅkukarṇa, holding a blazing club.
Bhṛṅgin of Hara's nature, and Vīrabhadra, and likewise hundreds of noble heroes among the lords of Gaṇas, / with thunderbolts, tridents, swords, and bhuśuṇḍi weapons in hand, filled with joy, stood eager to fight.
Seeing that chariot arrived, the Daityas, overcome by delusion, marched out to battle; / those heroic warriors headed by Tārakākṣa, arming themselves, their hands blazing with various weapons.
Overcome by anger, the sons of Danu fought a battle alongside the lords of the Gaṇas; / yet the god whose crest has the crescent moon as its abode did not discharge an arrow to burn down the city.
He merely stood repeatedly watching by himself that battle between his Gaṇas and the Daitya lords; / then Nandī, along with the heroic troop leaders of indomitable spirit, waged battle.

His eyes red with anger, Vidyutprabha pierced Bhṛṅgin with ten arrows; / but reaching Bhṛṅgin, those arrows were unable to cause him pain.
Then that Bhṛṅgiriṭi struck Vidyutprabha upon the back with a blazing trident; / struck by that trident, he reeled, and leaving Bhṛṅgin, fled afflicted with fear.
Thus broken, that lord of the Daityas, abandoning Bhṛṅgin, the foremost lord of Gaṇas, / pierced Vināyaka in the shoulder region with seven sharp, pointed arrows.
Again with seventy-three arrows Vidyutprabha struck him who has the face of a royal elephant / in his vital spots, having hit his mark; thereupon that lord of Vināyakas grew enraged.
Then that lion among lords of elephants, having wrapped the throat of the Daitya lord with the tip of his trunk, / tore his head from his body, like an elephant in rut [tears] a lotus from a lake.

7.17.m: 913 / A thousand divine years have elapsed, and this Tripura has not gone to destruction. / Discharge that blazing arrow, O Lord of gods; let those enemies of the gods go to ruin! / When the thousand years were fulfilled, Tripura converged, and again it became separated, O Lord of gods. / Yet the arrow was not loosed by you, O God of gods! Or what is the use of your yoga, O Lord of gods? / By mere intention of yours, O Lord, this Tripura, the residence of the daityas, goes to destruction. / If, however, I am to be honored, O Lord, loose that arrow at once against Tripura!"

7.17.m:
Addressed thus by the four-faced [Brahmā], the Slayer of the Bodiless One (Śiva) assumed the opposite stance
and, drawing that powerful bow, fitted that blazing arrow to Pināka.
By mere intention, the God, the creator and destroyer of the universe,
then brought together those three cities; and the world at once became motionless.
Consisting of Viṣṇu, feathered with Fire and Soma, blazing as if at the destruction of the three worlds,
the God then shot that terrible arrow; and having shot it, he said: “Alas! Woe!”
Then Nandī approached the Great Lord and, bowing down, spoke these words: “What [is this]?”
The Blessed Lord spoke to that Nandīśvara, wishing the welfare of his devotee Maya:
“Nandīśa, Viśvakarman is my devotee; so that the fire will not burn his city,
go by my command and turn away the fire and the two gods Soma and Hari.”
Then Nandī, receiving the command of the Lord of Gods, swiftly went to that city of Viśvakṛt;
[…] equal in speed, he went even before the blazing [arrow].
Seeing the Daitya-lord Maya there, with his body bowed to the Bull-bannered [Lord],
afflicted by fear of death and seeking refuge, Nandī comforted that devotee of Īśa:

7.17.m:
Resembling the fire of cosmic dissolution at the end of a yuga, blazing as if to destroy the world,
that fire, joined with Viṣṇu and the moon, reached the dwelling of Viśvakṛt; and Nandī,
by command of the Lord, immediately spoke these words: “O Fire, this is not to be burned!”
Then the fire spoke to that god: “Why must this not be burned by me?”
Nandī then spoke to the consumer of oblations: “Maya, a devotee of the Lord of Immortals, resides here.”
Fire quickly spoke to that king of the Asuras these words: “Come out swiftly, Maya!”
Taking a golden liṅga of the Great Lord, departing from the city, the Asura-lord Maya
swiftly entered Pātāla, rejoicing, paying homage to the beloved of Umā.
Nandīśvara too, having approached the side of the Lord of Gods and reported [everything], remained there.
Then Tripura became engulfed in flames, its buildings destroyed with machinery and bolts broken apart,
filled with the great, fierce cries uttered by many Asuras, teeming with the terrified wives of the Daitya chieftains.

7.17.m:
Moon-faced women with swelling breasts, standing at the windows of palaces and mansions,
asleep on couches, their eyes languid with passion, repeatedly watching the path of their lovers,
with eyes, with cosmetic pastes resembling copper, fair and slender, with broad hips—
those Daitya women saw themselves ablaze, embraced by the fire of the arrow.
Standing in the palaces, afflicted by fear, they fled in terror like Kinnara women on a mountain;
and then, looking up and seeing their lovers who had arrived, they embraced them and fell into a deep faint.
Then those sons of Diti, seizing their beloveds, their desires vanished, fled with haste;
and as soon as they went forth, confounded by the power of Śiva and bereft of strength, they fell into the ocean.

7.17.m:
Then huge fishes resembling mountains, fierce crocodiles, and terrible sea monsters
devoured those Daityas who had fallen into the ocean, their strength lost and bewildered.
And other great lords of aquatic creatures, with dreadful fangs and gaping mouths,
began to devour those fallen women, whose necklaces were broken and who were separated from their lovers.
Those fallen young women, being devoured, looking again and again at their lovers with anger,
greatly tormented by severe agony, wailed most pitifully.

That angry glance of those wanton Daitya women then shone intensely,
as if [the look] of women exhausted at the end of lovemaking by lovers wishing to go to another.
Then all the bulls among the Daityas, together with their wives, being consumed by the fire of Tripura,
sank into the ocean, torn to pieces by sea monsters, and, bereft of life, fell under the sway of death.

7.17.m:
And that arrow, whose essence was Agni, the Moon, and Janārdana, having burned that entire city of Tripura,
having thrown it into the ocean, reached quietude, was pacified, and returned to the hand of Śambhu. // 8.170.60
When those Daityas were slain and Tripura was burned, the god, the cause of creation, dissolution, and the rest,
again endowed the gods standing on the chariot with divine bodies, as before. // 61
Brahmā and the other lords of the heavenly dwellers bowed down, and then addressed this speech to the Lord:
"By you, O Blessed One, has this impossible, auspicious, great, and exceedingly terrible deed been done. // 62
The Daityas are slain; that Tripura is burned; peace has been brought to us, O Lord of gods and asuras.
Obeisance to you, who are always present everywhere, the creator of the gods, O supreme Lord!
Obeisance, obeisance to you who are all-pervading, whose motion and action are ever incomprehensible!" // 63
The god then said to those chiefs of the gods, headed by Brahmā, the Sun, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the Lord of Wealth:
"You must always be protected and guarded by me just like sons, O gods! // 64

7.17.m:
With your desires fulfilled and your enemies slain, go joyfully to your own abodes."
The gods then bowed down to the supreme god and went to their own dwellings. // 65
The god too, being praised by the Siddhas, together with the chiefs of the Gaṇas—
Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśvara, and Vīrabhadra—the three-eyed maker of the universe, went to the peak of Kailāsa. // 66
Thus has this unbearable deed of the God of gods,
known as the Burning of Tripura, been told to you by me, O Vyāsa.
Whatever human being, pure and devoted to Śarva, recites this,
becomes free of sin, a partaker of heaven, born among the gods. // 67
Thus in the Skandapurāṇa, in the Slaying of Tripura, ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter.
